title: Is Ownership the Best Metaphor for Learning? Education Potkalitsky, Nick
author: Potkalitsky, Nick
summary: Potkalitsky argues that 'ownership' -- the dominant metaphor in AI-era education discourse -- carries a hidden logic of property and transaction that undermines the constructivist intentions behind it. When learning is framed as ownership, the natural measure becomes whether knowledge was acquired and retained, not whether it transformed the learner. AI has made this flaw visible: a student who uses AI to produce an essay technically 'owns' the output by any transactional logic, yet something clearly essential is missing. A 2025 PNAS study found students using unguarded AI tutors scored 17% worse than non-AI students once access was removed. Potkalitsky proposes formation as a better frame, built on three stages: retention (holding knowledge without the source), transfer (applying knowledge in new contexts), and agency (acting from genuine understanding). Pedagogical design -- purpose-built AI tools, disciplinary instructional design, and transfer-demanding assessments -- determines which pathway students take.
points: The ownership metaphor sounds constructivist but carries property logic: it asks 'did the acquisition happen?' and measures via retention, quietly replacing the constructivist intention with a transactional one.

A 2025 PNAS study found students using unguarded AI tutors scored 17% worse on post-tests than students who used no AI -- they had the outputs but not the formation that the outputs were supposed to evidence.

Formation is a more accurate frame than ownership: genuine learning changes how you see, reason, and act -- it is not a transfer of possession but a trajectory through retention, transfer, and agency.

AI can augment or substitute for the learning process depending on design: when students generate first and use AI to pressure-test their thinking, formation occurs; when AI generates and students receive, it does not.

Disciplinary instructional design protects the core cognitive work of each subject -- close reading, source evaluation, proof construction -- while using AI at the periphery, preventing substitution of the moves that build formation.
quotes: Ownership is not a neutral word. It carries a logic -- the logic of property. You own something when it passes from outside you to inside you, when it becomes yours. Ownership implies a transaction, a moment of transfer, a before and after.

This is how a constructivist intention ends up producing a retention-based measure. The word ownership sounds like it is describing something the learner does. It is actually describing something the learner gets. The metaphor overrides the intention, quietly and almost invisibly, every time it is used.

The problem is not that the student failed to own the work. The problem is that ownership was never the right frame. What is missing is not possession. It is process -- the cognitive work that produces durable, flexible, actionable knowledge.

Students who used an unguarded AI tutor performed well during practice, then scored 17% worse than students who had never used AI at all once access was removed. They had the answers. They did not have the learning.
Formation is a better word than ownership. You are not the same after genuine learning as you were before. You see differently, reason differently, act differently. That is what the work is for.

Students who generate before they delegate carry something into the AI interaction that changes its character entirely. They have something to think with. Without that prior generation, AI doesn't augment thinking. It replaces it.

What determines which pathway a learner takes is mostly design -- the tools available, the tasks assigned, the evidence gathered. Purpose-built tools structure the interaction around the cognitive work of the discipline rather than the satisfaction of the prompt.
